items.title: The Kimwolf botnet is stalking your local network
items.raw_content: The story you are reading is a series of scoops nestled inside a far more urgent Internet-wide security advisory. The vulnerability at issue has been exploited for months already, and it’s time for a broader awareness of the threat. The short version is that everything you thought you knew about the security of the internal network behind your Internet router probably is now dangerously out of date. The security company Synthient currently sees more than 2 million infected Kimwolf devices distributed globally but with concentrations in Vietnam, Brazil, India, Saudi Arabia, Russia and the United States. Synthient found that two-thirds of the Kimwolf infections are Android TV boxes with no security or authentication built in.
items.title_zh: Kimwolf 僵尸网络正在窥探你的本地网络
items.summary: The security firm Synthient sees more than 2 million infected Kimwolf devices worldwide, concentrated in Vietnam, Brazil, India, Saudi Arabia, Russia and the United States, with two-thirds of the infections on Android TV boxes that have no built-in security or authentication. The flaw has already been exploited for months, the report says.

items.title: Recursive Language Models
items.raw_content: We study allowing large language models (LLMs) to process arbitrarily long prompts through the lens of inference-time scaling. We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt. We find that RLMs can successfully process inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows and, even for shorter prompts, dramatically outperform the quality of vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context and coding scaffolds (e.g., on GPT-5 by a median across the evaluated benchmarks of $26\%$ against compaction, $130\%$ against CodeAct with sub-calls, and $13\%$ against Claude Code) across four diverse long-context tasks while having comparable cost. At a small scale, we post-train the first mode
items.title_zh: 递归语言模型（Recursive Language Models）
items.summary: The paper introduces Recursive Language Models, an inference paradigm that treats long prompts as an external environment the model can examine, decompose and recursively query, handling inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond its context window. The authors report that it beat vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context or coding scaffolds across four long-context tasks at comparable cost, and that they post-trained an initial model at small scale.

items.title: Vector graphics on GPU
items.raw_content: Despite vector graphics being used in every computer with a screen connected to it, rendering of vector shapes and text is still mostly a task for the CPU. This is wrong and needs to be changed. Here I describe a general approach to rasterization and how we can ask for help from GPU when rendering vector paths. First, let's overview a general principle of rasterization of vector shapes. Here is an image with a clockwise circle in it and I'll demonstrate a very rudimentary algorithm for drawing one row of pixels of that image. For simplicity reasons, anti-aliasing will not be included at this time.
items.title_zh: 在 GPU 上渲染矢量图形
items.summary: The post argues that vector shape and text rendering is still mostly a CPU task and describes a general approach to rasterization that offloads vector path rendering to the GPU. Anti-aliasing is left out for simplicity.

items.title: X-Clacks-Overhead
items.raw_content: I am a big fan of Sir Terry Pratchett. His books influenced my sense of humor and the way I look at things, far beyond just fantasy literature. Some time ago, I added a small but meaningful detail to this blog - the X-Clacks-Overhead HTTP header. This header is a reference to the “Going Postal” novel and the Clacks system . In short, it is a quiet way to say “GNU Terry Pratchett” - a signal that keeps his name moving through the network, not forgotten.
